```{r setup}
library(targets)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
cfg      <- tar_read(config)
periods  <- tar_read(periods)
data_end <- tar_read(data_end)
xw       <- tar_read(crosswalk)
ck       <- xw$checks          # one row per city: composition, ratios, status
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(fmt(100 * x, d), "%")
kbl <- function(x, ...) knitr::kable(x, ...)
```

# Purpose and design

The published exposure-response functions (ERFs) of Masselot et al. (2023,
*Lancet Planetary Health*) are the standard source of temperature-mortality
risk for European cities, and the natural basis for a heat-mortality
forecasting system. This report asks whether they still describe mortality in
Italian cities after the period they were estimated on.

In 232 cities with observed daily mortality (for Italy, the MCC data covering 
2001-2010), a quasi-Poisson distributed-lag non-linear model was fitted; 
the city curves were then pooled in a meta-regression on city characteristics,
which was used to predict curves for all 854 cities. The paper does not include
an out-of-sample test over later years.

1. **Temperature forecast skill** — archived Open-Meteo forecasts
   (`r cfg$forecast_model`, leads `r min(cfg$forecast_leads)`-`r max(cfg$forecast_leads)`
   days) against ERA5-Land, to decide the usable horizon.
2. **Curve comparison** — Masselot's first-stage model refitted,
   with identical specification, on Istat deaths and ERA5-Land for
   `r periods$test$label`, and compared with the published curves
   `r if (!is.null(periods$repro)) paste0("(and for ", periods$repro$label, ", a period also independent of the Italian MCC data)") else ""`.
3. **Observed vs predicted heat deaths** — for heatwave episodes
   and whole summers, the heat deaths predicted by the curves are compared
   with the deaths observed above a counterfactual baseline of deaths
   expected without heat, for the published curves and for curves
   re-estimated on Italian data of an earlier period.
4. **Rolling recalibration** — for `r cfg$region_focus`, a curve refitted for
   every forecast month on the last `r cfg$rolling$train_years` years of
   deaths available before it (COVID-19 years skipped), scored out of sample
   against the published curves, with 95% prediction bands that flag
   abnormal mortality.

Italian published mortality data end on **`r format(data_end, "%d %B %Y")`**.

# Data and alignment

## Do we reproduce the paper's own numbers?

Code is run on paper's own exposure series (1990-2019) and his own annual deaths, 
and compared with the numbers published in `results.zip`. Minimum mortality 
temperatures come out identical and annual heat-attributable deaths are 
reproduced exactly.

```{r recon}
rc <- tar_read(recon_check)
kbl(rc[, .(`City x age` = .N,
           `Median MMT difference (°C)` = fmt(median(mmt_diff)),
           `Max |MMT difference|` = fmt(max(abs(mmt_diff))),
           `Median ratio of excess risk at P99` = fmt(median(rr_ratio), 3),
           `Median ratio of annual heat deaths` = fmt(median(heat_ratio), 3))],
    caption = "Our reconstruction vs the published results (1 = identical)")
```

```{r recon-plot, fig.height=4}
#| fig-cap: "Each point is a city and age group over 1990-2019."

ggplot(rc, aes(heat_pub, heat_ours, colour = agegroup)) + geom_abline(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = .7) + scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Annual heat deaths published by Masselot et al.", y = "Recomputed here",
       colour = "Age", title = "Reconstruction check, Italian cities, 1990-2019")
```

The `r nrow(tar_read(recon_check))` city-age combinations sit on the diagonal
across three orders of magnitude, from cities with a handful of heat deaths a
year to the largest. The pipeline therefore is the paper's pipeline.

## City definition

Original paper's cities are Urban Audit cities, coded with Eurostat's 2020/2021
numbering, in which the *greater city* is the default unit wherever the
urban centre extends well beyond the central municipality (e.g. Milan,
Naples): from the 2021 release greater cities are merged into the city
level, so a single "city" polygon can cover dozens of comuni.

The composition is taken from the source: Istat SITUAS portal, which lists every
Urban Audit city and the comuni that compose it, with their Istat codes:
`r format(nrow(tar_read(istat_cities)), big.mark = ",")` comuni in
`r data.table::uniqueN(tar_read(istat_cities)$city_code)` cities, of which
`r data.table::uniqueN(tar_read(istat_cities)[level == "greater city", city_code])`
greater cities. The table below shows the difference between original paper and 
this implementation sits below a reasonable difference.

```{r crosswalk-levels}
cnd <- attr(tar_read(istat_map), "candidates")
if (!is.null(cnd)) {
  w <- data.table::dcast(cnd[, .(city, variant, pop_ratio)], city ~ variant,
                         value.var = "pop_ratio")
  w <- w[!is.na(`greater city`)]
  data.table::setnames(w, c("City", "Core comune", "Greater city"))
  w[, Kept := data.table::fifelse(abs(log(`Core comune`)) <
                                    abs(log(`Greater city`)), "core comune", "greater city")]
  kbl(w[order(Kept, City), .(City, `Core comune` = fmt(`Core comune`),
                             `Greater city` = fmt(`Greater city`), Kept)],
      caption = "Population of each candidate level / population in Masselot's metadata")
}
```

The geographic matching this project started from is still computed as a
check: each city's Urban Audit point (from Masselot's metadata) is located
in the GISCO `r cfg$urau_year` polygons of every level
(`r paste(cfg$urau_levels, collapse = ", ")`); each polygon containing the
point is a candidate, made of the comuni with at least
`r pct(cfg$lau_share_min)` of their area inside it, and the candidate whose
population is closest to Masselot's is retained. The table below reports,
city by city, how far the two compositions agree. The retained composition
is then checked against the Istat deaths aged 20+ in 2011-2019 and the
deaths implied by Masselot's population structure and death rates: cities
failing this check are excluded, since their mortality would not be the
population the curve describes.

```{r crosswalk-agreement}
ag <- xw$checks[!is.na(agreement), .(City = name, Level = level,
                                     Comuni = n_comuni, `Comuni (geometric)` = n_comuni_geo,
                                     Shared = shared_comuni, Agreement = fmt(agreement))]
kbl(xw$checks[!is.na(agreement), .(Cities = .N,
      `Identical composition` = sum(agreement == 1),
      `Agreement below 0.9` = sum(agreement < 0.9))],
    caption = "Agreement between the official composition and the geometric matching")
dis <- ag[as.numeric(Agreement) < 1]
if (nrow(dis)) kbl(dis[order(as.numeric(Agreement))],
                   caption = "Cities where the two compositions differ")
```

```{r crosswalk-plot, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(ck[!is.na(deaths_ratio)], aes(pop_ratio, deaths_ratio, colour = status)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = cfg$pop_ratio_ok[1], xmax = cfg$pop_ratio_ok[2],
           ymin = cfg$deaths_ratio_ok[1], ymax = cfg$deaths_ratio_ok[2],
           alpha = .08, fill = "darkgreen") +
  geom_point(aes(size = pop), alpha = .7) +
  geom_text(data = ck[!is.na(deaths_ratio) & status != "ok"], aes(label = name),
            size = 3, vjust = -1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() + scale_size_area(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Population of the retained comuni / Masselot population",
       y = "Istat deaths 20+ / deaths implied by metadata",
       colour = NULL, title = "Alignment of city definitions (green = accepted range)")
```

```{r crosswalk-flagged}
#| tbl-cap-location: top

fl <- ck[status != "ok", .(City = name, Polygon = poly_name, Level = level, Status = status,
                           Candidates = n_candidates, `Pop. ratio` = fmt(pop_ratio),
                           `Deaths ratio` = fmt(deaths_ratio), Analysed = analysed)]
if (nrow(fl)) kbl(fl, caption = "Cities to inspect (a level or comuni can be forced in data/raw/crosswalk_overrides.csv)") else cat("All cities passed the checks.")
```

```{r crosswalk-outcome}
#| output: asis
nok  <- ck[status == "ok", .N]
ndth <- ck[status == "deaths differ from metadata rates", .N]
npop <- ck[status == "check population", .N]
nout <- ck[analysed == FALSE]
cat(sprintf(paste0("Of the %d cities in metadata, %d are carried into ",
                   "the analysis: %d pass every check, %d keep a deaths ratio outside the ",
                   "accepted band while their population matches (the regional death rates ",
                   "in his metadata, not a wrong city, so they stay with the flag) and %d ",
                   "are flagged on population only.\n\n"),
            nrow(ck), ck[analysed == TRUE, .N], nok, ndth, npop))
if (nrow(nout))
  cat(sprintf("Excluded: %s.\n\n",
              paste(sprintf("%s (%s)", nout$name, nout$status), collapse = "; ")))
```

## Age groups

Istat 5-year classes are merged into Masselot's groups (20-44, 45-64, 65-74,
75-84, 85+); deaths below age 20 are excluded, as in the paper.

```{r age-check}
ac <- tar_read(istat)$age_check
kbl(ac[, .(deaths = sum(deaths)), by = .(agegroup = fifelse(is.na(agegroup), "<20 (excluded)", agegroup))][
  , share := pct(deaths / sum(deaths), 1)], col.names = c("Age group", "Deaths (all years)", "Share"))
```

## Exposure

ERA5-Land daily mean temperature comes from Open-Meteo,
`r if (identical(cfg$era5_mode, "polygon")) sprintf("averaged over up to %d ERA5-Land cells inside each city polygon, as Masselot did", cfg$era5_max_points) else "taken at each city's point"`.
The two series are compared over `r format(cfg$overlap_start, "%Y")`-`r format(cfg$overlap_end, "%Y")`.
`r if (isTRUE(cfg$bias_correct)) "The city x month mean difference is removed from our series before any analysis, so temperatures sit on the scale of the distribution the ERF knots come from." else "No correction is applied."`

```{r exposure-check, fig.height=4}
ex <- tar_read(exposure_check)$summary
ex <- merge(ex, tar_read(cities)[, .(URAU_CODE, name)], by = "URAU_CODE")
kbl(ex[, .(Cities = .N, `Median bias (°C)` = fmt(median(bias)),
           `Max |bias| (°C)` = fmt(max(abs(bias))), `Median MAE (°C)` = fmt(median(mae)),
           `Median r` = fmt(median(r), 3))])
ggplot(ex, aes(bias, reorder(name, bias))) + geom_col(fill = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Mean difference, our point series - Masselot polygon series (°C)", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6))
```

```{r beyond-range}
#| include: true

td <- tar_read(erf)$tdist
pcs <- grep("%$", names(td), value = TRUE)
td[, tmax := do.call(pmax, .SD), .SDcols = pcs]
et <- merge(tar_read(exposure_test)[date >= periods$test$start], td[, .(URAU_CODE, tmax)], by = "URAU_CODE")
br <- et[, .(days = sum(tmean > tmax)), by = URAU_CODE][days > 0]
br <- merge(br, tar_read(cities)[, .(URAU_CODE, name)], by = "URAU_CODE")[order(-days)]
```

Averaging the cells inside each polygon brings the median difference to
`r fmt(ex[, median(bias)])` °C and the median daily error to
`r fmt(ex[, median(mae)])` °C, with a correlation of 1.000: our series and
the original one are effectively the same variable. What remains is topographic.
The largest positive differences are Trento, Cosenza and Bolzano, whose
polygons run up the surrounding slopes, so the city average is colder than
the built-up area; the largest negative ones, Lecco and Caserta, sit beside a
lake and a mountain range. The monthly mean difference removes what is left,
so the temperatures entering the curves are on the scale of the distribution
their knots come from.

In the test period, `r nrow(br)` cities had days warmer than the maximum of
their 1990-2019 distribution (`r sum(br$days)` city-days in total). On those
days both the published and the refitted curves are extrapolated beyond the
last spline knot, so relative risks there are uncertain; curves in the plots
below stop at the 1990-2019 maximum.

# Temperature forecast skill

```{r fc-setup}
fs <- tar_read(fc_skill)
# the three slices the text below quotes
sc <- fs$scores[subset == "Warm season"][order(lead)]
hd <- fs$scores[subset == "Hot days (> P90)"][order(lead)]
dt <- fs$detection[order(lead)]
```

Forecasts from the Open-Meteo Previous Runs API (value predicted N days
before the valid time; archive from `r format(cfg$forecast_start, "%B %Y")`)
are scored against ERA5-Land at the same point. The reference is persistence
(tomorrow = today): skill above 0 means the forecast beats it.

```{r fc-plot, fig.height=6}
# a different name: `sc` above is the warm-season slice the prose quotes
scl <- melt(fs$scores, id.vars = c("subset", "lead"), measure.vars = c("mae", "rmse", "bias", "mae_persistence"))
scl[, variable := factor(variable, c("mae", "rmse", "bias", "mae_persistence"),
                         c("MAE", "RMSE", "Bias", "MAE of persistence"))]
ggplot(scl, aes(lead, value, colour = variable)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~ subset) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = cfg$forecast_leads) +
  labs(x = "Lead time (days)", y = "°C", colour = NULL,
       title = "Error of daily mean temperature forecasts by lead time") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r fc-table}
kbl(fs$detection[, .(Lead = lead, Hits = hits, Misses = misses, `False alarms` = false_alarms,
                     POD = fmt(pod), FAR = fmt(far))],
    caption = sprintf("Detection of heatwave days (T >= P%s), warm season", cfg$hw_pct))
```

Forecast error grows slowly: the mean absolute error in the warm season is
`r fmt(sc$mae[1])` °C at one day and `r fmt(sc$mae[nrow(sc)])` °C at seven, and the
forecast beats persistence from day two onwards. On hot days it carries a warm
bias growing from `r fmt(hd$bias[1])` °C to `r fmt(hd$bias[nrow(hd)])` °C.
Heatwave days are detected reliably at every lead (probability of detection
`r fmt(min(dt$pod))`-`r fmt(max(dt$pod))`), at the cost of more false alarms as
the lead grows (`r fmt(min(dt$far))` to `r fmt(max(dt$far))`).

Most of this is bias rather than noise, so it can be removed: `fc_debias` in the
configuration subtracts the city, month and lead mean error, which should be
switched on before the forecasts are used to produce numbers rather than
warnings. With it on, the usable horizon is set by the growth in error, not
by the bias.

# Refitting the original first-stage model

In each city the model of Masselot's first stage is refitted exactly (script
`05_FirstStage.R` of the authors' repository): quasi-Poisson regression;
cross-basis with a quadratic B-spline of temperature (knots at the
10th/75th/90th percentiles and boundaries at the range of the city's
1990-2019 ERA5-Land distribution, i.e. the published basis) and a natural
spline of lags 0-`r cfg$lag_max` with `r cfg$lag_nknots` knots equally spaced
on the log scale; day-of-week indicators; natural spline of time with
`r cfg$df_time_per_year` df per year. The fit is reduced to the overall
cumulative curve, whose five coefficients are directly comparable with the
published ones. Series are all deaths 20+, and age groups merged with
Masselot's cumulative `r fmt(cfg$min_deaths, 0)`-death rule. The MMT is
searched between the `r cfg$mmp_range[1]`th and `r cfg$mmp_range[2]`th
percentiles, as in the paper.

The main comparison is the relative risk at the `r cfg$rr_pct`th percentile
versus the published MMT. Differences are pooled across cities with a 
random-effects meta-analysis.

```{r curve-fun}
show_curve_test <- function(ct, pooled, label) {
  r <- ct$results
  cat(sprintf("\n\n**%s.** %d cities fitted on all deaths 20+, %d not fitted (deaths below %s).\n\n",
              label, r[level == "all20" & status == "fitted", .N],
              r[level == "all20" & status != "fitted", .N], fmt(cfg$min_deaths, 0)))
  print(kbl(pooled[, .(Group = group, Cities = k,
                       `Ratio of RR99 (refit/published)` = fmt(ratio, 3),
                       `95% CI` = ifelse(is.na(lo), "", paste(fmt(lo, 3), "-", fmt(hi, 3))),
                       p = fmt(p, 3), `I²` = ifelse(is.na(i2), "", paste0(fmt(i2, 0), "%")))],
            caption = "Pooled difference in heat relative risk at P99 (1 = no difference)"))
}
forest_plot <- function(ct, pooled, label) {
  r <- ct$results[level == "all20" & status == "fitted"]
  r[, `:=`(lo = exp(d_lr99 - 1.96 * se_d_lr99), hi = exp(d_lr99 + 1.96 * se_d_lr99),
           src = fifelse(inmcc %in% TRUE, "Fitted on local data (MCC)", "Extrapolated"))]
  pool <- pooled[group == "All cities"]
  ggplot(r, aes(exp(d_lr99), reorder(name, d_lr99), colour = src)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey50") +
    annotate("rect", xmin = pool$lo, xmax = pool$hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
             alpha = .12, fill = "firebrick") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = pool$ratio, colour = "firebrick", linetype = 2) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0) + geom_point() +
    scale_x_log10() +
    labs(x = "RR99 refitted / RR99 published (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
         title = paste("City differences in heat risk,", label),
         subtitle = "Red band: pooled estimate and 95% CI") +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6), legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

## `r periods$test$label`

```{r test-a, results='asis'}
ct <- tar_read(curves_test); pt <- tar_read(pooled_test)
show_curve_test(ct, pt, periods$test$label)
```

```{r test-a-forest, fig.height=10}
forest_plot(ct, pt, periods$test$label)
```

The refitted coefficients are pooled in a multivariate meta-analysis and each 
city is represented by its best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP), which borrows
strength from the other cities in proportion to its own imprecision.

```{r test-a-curves, fig.height=9}
bt <- tar_read(blup_test)
if (!is.null(bt)) {
  top <- ct$results[level == "all20" & status == "fitted"][order(-deaths)][1:min(12, .N), URAU_CODE]
  b <- merge(bt$bands[URAU_CODE %in% top & curve != "Refitted (city only)"],
             tar_read(cities)[, .(URAU_CODE, name)], by = "URAU_CODE")
  ggplot(b, aes(t, rr, colour = curve, fill = curve)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = .15, colour = NA) + geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
    facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free_x") + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(.8, 2.5)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Published = "grey30", `Refitted (BLUP)` = "firebrick")) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Published = "grey30", `Refitted (BLUP)` = "firebrick")) +
    labs(x = "Daily mean temperature (°C), range observed in the period",
         y = "Relative risk (vs own MMT)", colour = NULL, fill = NULL,
         title = "Published and refitted (BLUP) curves, deaths 20+, largest cities") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

Heterogeneity between cities is small (I-squared of
`r fmt(pt[group == "All cities", i2], 0)`% in the test period), so this is a
common shift rather than a few outliers, and cities whose curves were fitted on
their own mortality show much the same gap as cities where the curve was
extrapolated from the meta-regression
(`r fmt(pt[grepl("MCC", group) & !grepl("Difference", group), ratio], 2)` against
`r fmt(pt[grepl("extrapolated", group) & !grepl("Difference", group), ratio], 2)`,
difference not significant).

The disagreement is confined to the heat arm. Above the minimum the refitted
curve rises much less steeply than the published one in every large city, and
the gap widens with temperature. However, the cold side it's confounded by
influenza, and it's not within the scope of this analysis.

```{r test-a-blup}
if (!is.null(bt)) kbl(bt$results[, .(Cities = .N, `Median RR99 published` = fmt(median(rr99_pub), 3),
                                    `Median RR99 refitted (BLUP)` = fmt(median(rr99_blup), 3),
                                    `Median ratio` = fmt(exp(median(d_lr99)), 3))],
                      caption = "Heat relative risk at P99 vs the published MMT, BLUP curves")
```

```{r test-a-mmt, fig.height=4.5}
r <- ct$results[status == "fitted"]
print(ggplot(r[level == "all20"], aes(af_pub, af_new)) + geom_abline(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = af_new - 1.96 * se_d_af, ymax = af_new + 1.96 * se_d_af),
                colour = "grey70", width = 0) + geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Heat-attributable fraction, published curve", y = "Refitted curve",
       title = sprintf("Heat-attributable fraction of deaths 20+, %s", periods$test$label)))
```

```{r test-a-repro, results='asis'}
if (isTRUE(cfg$run_reproduction)) {
cat("\n\n## ", periods$repro$label, "\n\n")
cat("This period uses Masselot's original ERA5-Land series, so the only difference ",
    "with the published model is the mortality data. For Italian MCC cities the ",
    "published curves used 2001-2010 data, so these years are independent too; ",
    "for extrapolated cities this is a direct test of the spatial prediction ",
    "over the period the curves describe.\n\n")
cr <- tar_read(curves_repro); pr <- tar_read(pooled_repro)
show_curve_test(cr, pr, periods$repro$label)
}
```

```{r test-a-repro-forest, fig.height=10}
if (isTRUE(cfg$run_reproduction)) forest_plot(cr, pr, periods$repro$label)
```

## Trend across time windows

The same first-stage model is refitted in successive windows. Windows ending
before 2020 use Masselot's own ERA5-Land series, so the exposure is identical
to his; later windows use our aligned series. A falling ratio means the heat
risk carried by the published curves is increasingly too steep for the data.

```{r periods}
cp <- tar_read(curves_periods)
kbl(cp$pooled[, .(Window = window, Cities = k, `Ratio of RR99 (refit/published)` = fmt(ratio, 3),
                  `95% CI` = paste(fmt(lo, 3), "-", fmt(hi, 3)), p = fmt(p, 3))],
    caption = "Pooled difference with the published curves, by time window")
if (!is.null(cp$trend))
  kbl(cp$trend[, .(`Change per decade` = fmt(change_per_decade, 3),
                   `95% CI` = paste(fmt(lo, 3), "-", fmt(hi, 3)), p = fmt(p, 3))],
      caption = "Meta-regression of the difference on the window midpoint")
```

```{r periods-plot, fig.height=4}
if (nrow(cp$pooled)) {
  ggplot(cp$pooled, aes(midyear, ratio)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = .3, colour = "grey50") +
    geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "firebrick") +
    geom_text(aes(label = window), vjust = -1.4, size = 3) +
    labs(x = "Midpoint of the window", y = "Refitted / published heat risk at P99",
         title = "Is the gap widening over time?")
}
```

The ratio falls in every step, and the trend is significant. Two of the three
windows use original paper's own temperatures, so the decline shouldn't be an
artefact of a different exposure series.

# One region in full: `r cfg$region_focus`

Everything above tests the cities that carry enough deaths for original paper's
first stage: 5,000 over the period. An operational system needs a curve for
*every* city of the region it covers, small ones included. A city whose own fit 
is noisy enters the multivariate random-effects meta-analysis with a large 
variance, so its best linear unbiased prediction sits close to the pooled 
Italian curve: it contributes what its own data support and borrows the rest. 
The pooling here uses every Italian city fitted in the test period, not only the
region's, and the first stage is the same model with the same knots — only the
death threshold is lifted.

```{r region-table}
rt <- tar_read(region_table)
if (is.null(rt) || !nrow(rt)) cat("No city of this region is in the analysis.\n") else {
  tb <- rt[, .(City = name,
               `Deaths 20+ in the period` = fmt(deaths, 0),
               `Own fit` = fifelse(is.na(deaths), "-",
                 fifelse(below_threshold, "below threshold", "above threshold")),
               `RR99 published` = fmt(rr99_pub, 3),
               `RR99 own fit` = sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", fmt(rr99_own, 2),
                                        fmt(rr99_own_lo, 2), fmt(rr99_own_hi, 2)),
               `RR99 BLUP` = sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", fmt(rr99_blup, 2),
                                     fmt(rr99_blup_lo, 2), fmt(rr99_blup_hi, 2)),
               MCC = fifelse(inmcc, "yes", "no"))]
  kbl(tb, caption = sprintf(paste("Heat relative risk at the 99th percentile vs the published",
                                  "MMT, %s, %s"), cfg$region_focus, periods$test$label))
}
```

# Observed vs predicted heat deaths

**Deaths expected without heat.** For every city and age group a baseline
is estimated: a quasi-Poisson model with day of week, a slow trend and
`r cfg$baseline_harmonics` annual harmonics, fitted only on *reference days*
— outside the influenza season (months
`r paste(month.abb[cfg$baseline_exclude_months], collapse = ", ")`) and not
within `r cfg$baseline_hot_lag` days after a day above the curve's MMT. Like
EuroMOMO baselines, it captures the normal seasonal pattern, including the
lower mortality of summer, without the heat itself. Reference days are cool, so 
part of their deaths is cold-related: `r if (isTRUE(cfg$baseline_cold_offset)) "the published cold effect enters the model as an offset, so B is the number of deaths expected at the minimum-mortality temperature, the reference of the attributable-deaths formula" else "no correction is applied, so B also contains cold-related deaths"`. Age groups with fewer than `r cfg$baseline_min_daily`
deaths per day use the 20+ baseline times their share.

Over each window:

- **Observed heat deaths** X = observed deaths − Baseline;
- **Predicted heat deaths** P = Σ Baseline × (RR − 1) over the days at or above the
  MMT, with the relative risk centred on the MMT. Days below the MMT inside a
  window belong to the cold side of the curve and are counted separately.

Windows are heatwave episodes (spells of at least `r cfg$hw_min_days` days above the
city's P`r cfg$hw_pct`, plus `r cfg$tail_days` days), and whole summers
(June-September), which do not depend on any episode definition.
Uncertainty of both the baseline and the curves is propagated.

```{r test-b-setup}
cf <- tar_read(counterfactual); ev <- tar_read(cf_eval)
has_ep <- !is.null(ev)
```

**Timing check.** Before comparing numbers, the dates themselves are
checked: within each city and summer, daily excess deaths (observed − B)
are correlated with the temperature of k days earlier. Deaths should follow
the heat by 0-2 days; a peak at a negative shift would mean deaths come
before the temperature that causes them, i.e. a date error somewhere
between the Istat file and the temperature series.

```{r timing-check, fig.height=3.5}
tc <- Filter(Negate(is.null), tar_read(timing_check))
if (length(tc)) {
  cc <- rbindlist(lapply(names(tc), function(p) cbind(period = p, tc[[p]]$ccf)))
  pk <- cc[, .SD[which.max(r)], by = period]
  print(ggplot(cc, aes(lag, r, colour = period)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
    geom_line() + geom_point(data = pk, size = 2.5) +
    labs(x = "Days by which deaths follow temperature (negative = deaths first)",
         y = "Correlation of excess deaths\nwith temperature", colour = NULL) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
  eo <- rbindlist(lapply(names(tc), function(p) if (!is.null(tc[[p]]$episodes))
    cbind(period = p, tc[[p]]$episodes)))
}
```

`r if (length(tc)) sprintf("The correlation peaks at %s. %s", paste(sprintf("%+d days (%s)", pk$lag, pk$period), collapse = " and "), if (nrow(eo)) sprintf("Episode by episode, excess deaths peak a median of %s days after the hottest days (%s of the %d episodes peak before them%s).", fmt(median(eo$offset), 0), pct(mean(eo$offset < 0)), nrow(eo), if (any(eo$offset < 0) && any(eo$offset >= 0)) sprintf("; those last a median of %s days, against %s for the others", fmt(median(eo[offset < 0, ndays]), 0), fmt(median(eo[offset >= 0, ndays]), 0)) else "") else "") else ""`
A peak at 0 to +2 days says the dates are aligned. Within that, deaths can
still peak before the hottest days of a *long* episode without any date
error: the people most vulnerable to heat die in its first days, and later
days of the same heat find fewer of them (depletion), all the more in the
first heat of the season. The curves have no memory of how long the heat
has lasted, so they predict the same risk for the same temperature and peak
with the temperature.

```{r test-b-example, fig.height=4.5}
if (has_ep) {
  big <- ev$windows[type == "summer"][order(-O)][1]
  dd <- cf$daily[URAU_CODE == big$URAU_CODE & date >= big$start & date <= big$end,
                 .(O = sum(deaths), B = sum(B), E = sum(B * exp(logrr))), by = date]
  nm <- tar_read(cities)[URAU_CODE == big$URAU_CODE, name]
  dd <- melt(dd, id.vars = "date")
  dd[, variable := factor(variable, c("O", "B", "E"),
                          c("Observed", "Expected without heat (B)", "Predicted with published curve"))]
  print(ggplot(dd, aes(date, value, colour = variable)) +
    geom_line(data = dd[variable == "Observed"], alpha = .5) +
    geom_line(data = dd[variable != "Observed"], linewidth = .9) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "steelblue", "firebrick")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths per day (20+)", colour = NULL,
         title = sprintf("%s, summer %s", nm, big$year)) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
}
```

# Curves re-estimated on Italian data

The published curves are re-estimated on Italian mortality of an earlier
window, with Masselot's own temperatures and his own model, then pooled and
shrunk exactly as in his second stage. Applied to the test period they are
out of sample, since no data after the window enters them. The comparison
below keeps the baseline and every other choice fixed, so it isolates the
effect of the curve itself.

```{r curve-sets}
cs <- tar_read(curve_sets)
kbl(cs$calibration[, .(Windows = fifelse(windows == "episode", "Episodes", "Summers"),
                       Curves = curves, N = n, Observed = fmt(observed, 0),
                       Predicted = fmt(predicted, 0), `Observed / predicted` = fmt(ratio),
                       Slope = sprintf("%s (%s-%s)", fmt(slope), fmt(lo), fmt(hi)),
                       r = fmt(r))],
    caption = "Calibration of published and re-estimated curves (slope 1 = calibrated)")
```

```{r curve-set-numbers}
cse <- cs$calibration[windows == "episode"]
pubr <- cse[curves == "Published (Masselot et al.)"]
recr <- cse[curves != "Published (Masselot et al.)"][order(-ratio)]
```

Re-estimating the level closes most of the gap: the ratio of observed to
predicted goes from `r fmt(pubr$ratio)` with the published curves to
`r paste(sprintf("%s (%s)", fmt(recr$ratio), recr$curves), collapse = " and ")`,
and the slope from `r fmt(pubr$slope)` to
`r paste(fmt(recr$slope), collapse = " and ")`. Which window fits best is
itself informative: a later window fitting better says risk kept falling after
2019, while a longer window fitting better says the shorter one is too noisy.

The slope stays below 1 even where the totals match, so the largest episodes
are still over-predicted relative to the small ones — worth remembering for a
warning system, where the largest episodes are the ones that matter.

```{r example-plot, fig.height=7}
ex <- tar_read(example)
if (!is.null(ex)) {
  d <- ex$data[!is.na(deaths)]
  ggplot(d[series != "Observed"], aes(date, deaths, colour = series)) +
    geom_line(data = d[series == "Observed"], colour = "grey55", alpha = .6, linewidth = .4) +
    geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
    facet_wrap(~ year, ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(
      c("steelblue", "firebrick", c("#1B7837", "#762A83", "#B35806"))[
        seq_len(uniqueN(d[series != "Observed", series]))],
      levels(droplevels(d[series != "Observed", series])))) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths per day (20+)", colour = NULL,
         title = sprintf("%s: observed deaths, baseline and predictions", ex$city),
         subtitle = "Grey: observed. Summers of the test period") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

# Rolling recalibration: `r cfg$region_focus`

```{r roll-setup}
rl <- tar_read(rolling); re <- tar_read(roll_eval); rx <- tar_read(roll_example)
has_roll <- !is.null(rl) && nrow(rl$windows) > 0 && !is.null(re)
rc <- cfg$rolling
nm_city <- tar_read(cities)[, .(URAU_CODE, name)]
PUBLISHED_LABEL <- if (!is.null(re)) re$curve_sets[1] else "Published (Masselot et al.)"
```

A fixed window freezes the level of heat risk at the date it ends, and the
previous sections show that level kept falling. Here the curves are never
frozen: for every target month (`r paste(month.abb[rc$target_months], collapse = ", ")`)
Masselot's first stage is refitted on the last `r rc$train_years` years of
Istat deaths available *before* that month (`r if (identical(rc$update, "yearly")) "updated once a year, on the deaths up to 31 December" else "updated every month, on the deaths up to the end of the previous month"`),
skipping `r paste(range(rc$skip_years), collapse = "-")` because of COVID-19,
and the city fits are pooled and shrunk as in the second stage
(`r if (identical(rc$pool, "italy")) "every Italian city with enough deaths in the window enters the meta-analysis, and the region's cities are always fitted, whatever their size" else "only the region's cities enter the meta-analysis"`).
A target whose training years would start before the first Istat year is not
predicted. The published curves stay the reference: the question is whether
a curve that tracks the most recent mortality predicts the next month's heat
deaths better than a curve fitted on 2001-2010.

Every curve is out of sample for the month it is used in, so the scores
below are what a forecaster would have obtained at the time. The pre-COVID
years are scored as well, with the same baseline model and Masselot's own
temperatures; the fixed recalibrated curves of the previous section are
fitted on those years, so they are compared only in the post-COVID period,
where they are out of sample too.

```{r roll-targets, results='asis'}
if (!is.null(rl)) {
  st <- rl$targets[, .(Months = .N, First = min(key), Last = max(key)), by = .(Status = status)]
  print(kbl(st, caption = "Target months and their status"))
  cat("\n\n")
  if (nrow(rl$windows)) {
    w <- rl$windows[c(1, .N)]
    print(kbl(w[, .(`Window ends` = train_end, `Training days` = label,
                    `Cities pooled` = n_pooled, Pooling = method)],
              caption = "First and last training window"))
  }
}
```

```{r roll-trajectory, fig.height=7}
#| fig-cap: "Heat relative risk at P99 (vs the curve's own MMT) of the curve in force in each target month. Grey: 95% interval of the BLUP. Dashed: the published curves, weighted by the window's deaths by age."
if (has_roll && nrow(rl$summary)) {
  s <- merge(rl$summary, nm_city, by = "URAU_CODE")
  s[, era := train_end < as.Date(sprintf("%d-01-01", min(rc$skip_years)))]
  print(ggplot(s, aes(train_end + 1, rr99, group = era)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey80") +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = rr99_lo, ymax = rr99_hi), fill = "grey80") +
    geom_line(aes(y = rr99_pub), colour = "firebrick", linetype = 2) +
    geom_line(colour = "grey20") + geom_point(aes(shape = source), size = 1.2) +
    facet_wrap(~ name) +
    labs(x = "Month the curve is used for", y = "RR at P99", shape = "Curve") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
}
```

  allp <- tail(re$periods, 1)
  g <- function(sub, cur, ty = "episode")
    re$calibration[period == allp & subset == sub & type == ty & curves == cur]
  pub_all <- g("All windows", PUBLISHED_LABEL); rol_all <- g("All windows", rl$label)
  pub_lg <- g("Large episodes", PUBLISHED_LABEL); rol_lg <- g("Large episodes", rl$label)

`r if (has_roll && ok_num) sprintf("Over %s (%d episodes of the region), the published curves predict %s heat deaths against %s observed (ratio %s, slope %s); the rolling curves predict %s (ratio %s, slope %s), and %s of the episodes fall inside their 95%% prediction interval against %s with the published curves.", if (allp == "All periods") "all the years scored" else allp, rol_all$n, fmt(pub_all$predicted, 0), fmt(pub_all$observed, 0), fmt(pub_all$ratio), fmt(pub_all$slope), fmt(rol_all$predicted, 0), fmt(rol_all$ratio), fmt(rol_all$slope), pct(rol_all$coverage_95), pct(pub_all$coverage_95)) else ""`
`r if (has_roll && ok_lg) sprintf("On the large episodes - the ones a warning system exists for - the ratio of observed to predicted goes from %s with the published curves to %s with the rolling ones (slope %s to %s, mean absolute error %s to %s deaths per episode).", fmt(pub_lg$ratio), fmt(rol_lg$ratio), fmt(pub_lg$slope), fmt(rol_lg$slope), fmt(pub_lg$mae, 1), fmt(rol_lg$mae, 1)) else ""`

The calibration chart keeps only the episodes that matter for a warning:
those whose observed deaths rose above the grey band of deaths expected
without heat (the upper end of its 95% range), i.e. a significant excess.
Selecting on the observed deaths favours episodes where chance pushed deaths
up, so on this subset any set of curves looks a little low; the comparison
between the two sets is what matters here, and the warning table at the end
of the report scores all episodes, with or without excess.

```{r roll-scatter, fig.height=5.5}
if (has_roll) {
  keep_sets <- c(PUBLISHED_LABEL, rl$label)

  w[, curves := factor(curves, keep_sets)]
  sl <- re$calibration[period == tail(re$periods, 1) & type == "episode" &
                         subset == "Episodes with significant excess" & curves %in% keep_sets]
  sl[, curves := factor(curves, keep_sets)]
  print(ggplot(w, aes(P, X)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey85") +
    geom_abline(colour = "grey40", linetype = 2) +
    geom_abline(data = sl, aes(slope = slope, intercept = 0), colour = "firebrick") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = pi_lo - B, ymax = pi_hi - B), colour = "grey80", width = 0) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = size, shape = abnormal), alpha = .8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Large = "firebrick", Other = "grey40")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(above = 17, below = 25, within = 16)) +
    facet_wrap(~ curves, nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Predicted heat deaths", y = "Observed heat deaths (O - B)",
         colour = "Episode", shape = "Observed vs 95% PI",
         title = sprintf("Episodes with a significant excess of deaths (%d)", uniqueN(w$id)),
         subtitle = paste("Dashed = perfect calibration; red = fitted slope. Vertical bars:",
                          "95% prediction range of the heat deaths")) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom"))
}
```

}

The figure below is what the app shows as a grey band: for every summer
day, the 95% prediction interval of the deaths expected with the rolling
curve in force that day - uncertainty of the curve, of the baseline level,
and the day-to-day noise of the counts. Days whose observed deaths fall
outside it are marked: those are abnormal for what the curve expects, either
because the heat effect was larger than predicted (above) or because
something other than heat, or a heat effect smaller than predicted, kept
deaths down (below). In a calibrated system about 2.5% of days fall on each
side.

# Interpretation and limitations

```{r interpretation, results='asis'}
pt <- tar_read(pooled_test); cp <- tar_read(curves_periods)
ep <- ev$calibration[windows == "Heatwave episodes"]
rec <- cs$calibration[windows == "episode" & curves != "Published (Masselot et al.)"]
best <- rec[which.min(abs(ratio - 1))]
cat(sprintf(paste0(
"**The published curves are too steep for Italy today.** Our reconstruction ",
"reproduces the paper's own numbers exactly, the cities are aligned to the ",
"population the curves describe, and the temperatures are Masselot's variable. ",
"On that footing, refitting his first-stage model on Italian data gives heat ",
"risks at the 99th percentile %s times the published ones (95%% CI %s-%s), and ",
"counting deaths against a baseline of expected deaths gives a calibration ",
"slope of %s (%s-%s). Over the test period the published curves predict %s heat ",
"deaths against %s observed. The two tests share only the published curves, and ",
"they agree.\n\n"),
fmt(pt[group == "All cities", ratio], 3), fmt(pt[group == "All cities", lo], 3),
fmt(pt[group == "All cities", hi], 3), fmt(ep$slope), fmt(ep$lo), fmt(ep$hi),
fmt(ep$predicted, 0), fmt(ep$observed, 0)))

cat(sprintf(paste0(
"**The gap is not a shape problem and not a place problem.** The refitted ",
"curves track the published ones along the cold arm and separate from them ",
"only above the minimum mortality temperature; heterogeneity between cities is ",
"small; and cities whose curves came from their own mortality behave like ",
"cities where the curve was extrapolated. What is out of date is the level of ",
"heat risk. Window by window the ratio falls: %s, a change of ",
"%s per decade (95%% CI %s-%s, p = %s), with the two earlier windows using ",
"Masselot's own temperatures. The Italian mortality behind the published ",
"curves ends in 2010 and includes the 2003 heatwave, so these curves describe ",
"a population that was more vulnerable to heat than today's.\n\n"),
paste(sprintf("%s in %s", fmt(cp$pooled$ratio, 3), cp$pooled$window), collapse = ", "),
fmt(cp$trend$change_per_decade, 3), fmt(cp$trend$lo, 3), fmt(cp$trend$hi, 3),
fmt(cp$trend$p, 3)))
```

Limitations:

- **Place of residence.** Istat counts deaths by comune of residence, not of
  occurrence, as do the mortality series used by Masselot et al.
- **Exposure.** Our series is taken at the city point, Masselot's is a
  city-polygon average; the difference is measured and
  `r if (isTRUE(cfg$bias_correct)) "removed as a monthly mean" else "not corrected"`.
  Forecasts come from a coarser model grid than ERA5-Land.
- **Power.** With about three and a half years, small cities cannot support
  the first-stage model and are left to the pooled analyses and test B.
- **Post-pandemic period.** 2023 still carried residual effects of
  COVID-19 and of the mortality deficit that followed it; the spline of time
  absorbs slow changes but not short epidemics during episodes.
- **Rolling curves.** `r cfg$rolling$train_years` years of deaths are few for
  a city on its own: small cities' rolling curves are mostly the pooled
  curve, and the cold arm of a window is confounded by influenza (only the
  heat arm is used for the heat deaths). The first post-COVID windows join
  2017-2019 to the first months of 2023, so they mix two populations.

# Heatwave warnings: significant excess, observed and predicted

```{r warn-setup}
has_warn <- has_roll && !is.null(re$warnings) && nrow(re$warnings) > 0
warn_sets <- if (has_roll) c(PUBLISHED_LABEL, rl$label) else character()
```

The question a warning system answers is binary: will this heatwave push
deaths above what is normal? For every heatwave episode of
`r cfg$region_focus` (`r if (has_roll) paste(head(re$periods, -1), collapse = " and ") else ""`):

- a **significant excess was observed** when the episode's deaths exceeded the
  upper end of the 95% range of deaths expected without heat (the grey band
  of the app around the expectation: baseline level uncertainty plus the
  noise of the counts);
- a **significant excess was predicted** when the deaths expected with the
  curves (baseline × relative risk) exceeded that same bound.

The predictions use the temperatures that actually occurred, so this is the
skill of the curves given a perfect temperature forecast; forecast errors
come on top (section 3).

```{r warn-matrix, results='asis'}
if (has_warn) {
  ap <- tail(re$periods, 1)
  for (cs in warn_sets) {
    x <- re$warnings[period == ap & curves == cs]
    if (!nrow(x)) next
    m <- data.table(` ` = c("Excess predicted", "No excess predicted"),
                    `Excess observed` = c(x$hits, x$misses),
                    `No excess observed` = c(x$false_alarms, x$correct_negatives),
                    Total = c(x$hits + x$false_alarms, x$misses + x$correct_negatives))
    print(kbl(m, caption = sprintf("%s, %s: %d episodes", cs,
                                   if (ap == "All periods") "all years scored" else ap, x$n)))
    cat("\n\n")
  }
}
```

```{r warn-scores, results='asis'}
if (has_warn) {
  ws <- re$warnings[curves %in% warn_sets]
  print(kbl(ws[, .(Period = period, Curves = curves, Episodes = n, Hits = hits,
                   `False alarms` = false_alarms, Misses = misses,
                   `Correct negatives` = correct_negatives,
                   POD = fmt(pod), FAR = fmt(far), CSI = fmt(csi), Bias = fmt(bias),
                   PSS = fmt(pss), HSS = fmt(hss))],
            caption = paste("Warning scores. POD: share of observed excesses that were",
                            "predicted (1 = none missed). FAR: share of predicted excesses",
                            "that did not happen (0 = no false alarms). CSI: hits / (hits +",
                            "misses + false alarms). Bias: predicted / observed events",
                            "(1 = as many warnings as events). PSS and HSS: skill against",
                            "chance (0 = no skill, 1 = perfect).")))
  wr <- re$warnings[period == tail(re$periods, 1) & curves == rl$label]
  wp <- re$warnings[period == tail(re$periods, 1) & curves == PUBLISHED_LABEL]
}
```

`r if (has_warn && nrow(wr) && nrow(wp)) sprintf("With the rolling curves, %d of the %d episodes with a significant excess were predicted (POD %s, against %s with the published curves), and %s of the warnings would have been false alarms (FAR %s against %s). The published curves warn %s times as often as excesses happen, the rolling ones %s times.", wr$hits, wr$hits + wr$misses, fmt(wr$pod), fmt(wp$pod), pct(wr$far), fmt(wr$far), fmt(wp$far), fmt(wp$bias), fmt(wr$bias)) else ""`

```{r warn-list}
if (has_warn) {
  w <- merge(re$windows[type == "episode" & curves %in% warn_sets], nm_city, by = "URAU_CODE")
  oc <- function(o, f) fifelse(o & f, "Hit", fifelse(o & !f, "Missed",
                         fifelse(!o & f, "False alarm", "")))
  pub <- w[curves == PUBLISHED_LABEL, .(period, id, name, start, end, O, nh_hi, X,
                                        obs_sig, P_pub = P, out_pub = oc(obs_sig, fc_sig))]
  rol <- w[curves == rl$label, .(period, id, P_roll = P, lo = pi_lo - B, hi = pi_hi - B,
                                 out_roll = oc(obs_sig, fc_sig))]
  wl <- merge(pub, rol, by = c("period", "id"))[
    obs_sig | out_pub != "" | out_roll != ""][order(start, name)]
  kbl(wl[, .(name, start, end, fmt(O, 0), fmt(nh_hi, 0), fmt(X, 0),
             fifelse(obs_sig, "yes", "no"), fmt(P_pub, 0), out_pub, fmt(P_roll, 0),
             sprintf("%s to %s", fmt(lo, 0), fmt(hi, 0)), out_roll)],
      col.names = c("City", "Start", "End", "Observed", "No-heat upper bound",
                    "Observed heat deaths", "Significant excess", "Published",
                    "Published: warning", "Rolling", "Rolling: 95% range",
                    "Rolling: warning"),
      caption = paste("Every episode with a significant excess observed or predicted by either",
                      "set of curves. Observed: deaths in the episode window (episode +",
                      cfg$tail_days, "days). Published / Rolling: predicted heat deaths."))
}
```
